title: Munchausen syndrome by proxy: a case report
case_prompt:
An 18-month-old Saudi girl was referred for evaluation of recurrent hypoglycemic episodes. She was born at term via cesarean section with a birth weight of 1.0 kg after a pregnancy complicated by maternal gestational diabetes and required 2 months of NICU care for respiratory distress. She met developmental milestones appropriately until age 9 months, when she developed generalized tonic–clonic seizures without fever, lasting 2–3 minutes. A 6-year-old brother has epilepsy.

At 13 months, she became lethargic, drowsy, and irritable; blood glucose measurement revealed hypoglycemia, and she was discharged on dietary recommendations. She then had another seizure and decreased consciousness; a local hospital PICU admission showed a blood glucose level of 30 mg/dL treated with intravenous fluids. On referral, she required high concentrations of dextrose (up to 25%), frequent high-dose octreotide, and glucagon.

Multiple samples during hypoglycemia demonstrated serum glucose 4.0 mmol/L, insulin 3744 pmol/L, and C-peptide 0.02 ng/mL. Physical examination revealed a swelling with needle-insertion marks on the upper lateral right thigh and bilateral deltoid needle marks; the child remained calm during needle pricks. The mother insisted on pancreatectomy. All other investigations—including genetic testing, PET imaging of the pancreas, brain MRI, and EEG—were unremarkable. All hypoglycemic episodes occurred while the mother was present, raising suspicion of an exogenous cause of hypoglycemia.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia of infancy — “An initial clue to PHHI as a differential diagnosis is an extremely high birth weight averaging around 3.7 kg, with all other physical findings being normal. On the contrary, in our case, the patient was born with a low birth weight of 1 kg.”  
2. Infant of diabetic mother — “Other diseases, which also present with an increased birth weight include: infants of diabetic mothers and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.”  
3. Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome — “Those can be differentiated from PHHI with the presence of other features, such as macroglossia, macrosomia, ear pits, omphalocele, hemihyperplasia, visceromegaly, renal abnormalities, and embryonal tumors in Beckwith-Weidmann syndrome.”  
4. Insulinoma — “The two most common causes of this disease are congenital hyperinsulinism (CHI) and insulinoma … The genetic testing and PET scan in our patient were normal.”  
5. Caregiver-fabricated illness (factitious hypoglycemia) — “The triad of hypoglycemia, hyperinsulinemia, and low C-peptide supports our diagnosis of the factitious hypoglycemic disorder.”
